It's a rich experience. Pretty heavy-handed with the message but it's the little sidebar stories, if you will, that give it depth. Except for Juliet, I really got invested in the characters. It's basically a glorified choose-your-own adventure book. Lots of reading. Know what you're getting into before you buy the game, because it is not a game for the masses. For the right person looking to experience the other side of NSA paranoia, however - this is going to be a fun ride.

Pros:
- The achievements are super clever in execution. They help to illuminate where the stories diverge, making your second playthrough a charming foray through a new line of consequences.
- You can literally choose between being a benevolent buddy and a snitching tyrant. You decide the fates of these characters. It's a pretty heady power trip.
- The music cues, while a little hokey, are still a nice touch.
- This game doesn't use typical time restraints. It's not a rush to the finish line. You choose when to end the day. Together with the music, it's a more laid-back atmosphere.

Cons:
- The interface is a little unweildy. Trying to sift through the character web gets super annoying when swapping back and forth between individual storylines.
- The experience is super streamlined, so there's really very little point in another playthrough after you unlock all of the achievements.
- This game likes to hold your hand. It literally tells you which pages are important to progressing the story. It has a predefined arc that refuses to progress until you upload the right piece of information. Really takes away any illusion of organic play.
- The act 5 reveal literally comes out of nowhere.

Conclusions: it's a deeply flawed game and it's not for everybody. But for the right person, it's well worth the price of admission, especially if it's on sale.

8/10 - A compelling detective story that questions your morals, tugs your heart strings, and leaves you stunned
+ Intriguing plot that keeps you telling yourself "just one more episode, sleep is not THAT important..."
+ Interesting characters who are easy to become attached to
+ Intellectually satisfying.  The game expects to absorb the world it has built and use deductive reasoning to back up your decisions and lines of investigation.  It doesn't treat you like an idiot (which I can appreciate)

- Fairly short game play (Start to finish is roughly 5-7 hours)
- Currently (Dec 5, 2016), no revising chapters and changing decisions.  You have to create a new save from the beginning to pick different choices (developers have stated that they will change this in the near future).

Note that this game plays similar to a detective visual novel.  If you are looking for flashy cut-scenes and first/third person character control, this is not the game for you.  You are an intelligence agent working at your computer, and that is how you will experience this world.  In my opinion, you do not need fancy graphics to appreciate the depth of this amazing story.

Wow, just wow. I just finished this game and loved every minute of it. I bought this game expecting more of an open-world investigative type game but got a pretty good story that tied together very nicely.

You play as "The Investigator", responsible for combing through information relating to Persons of Interest in a particular case. You're paired with an "Advisor", who goes through the data you provide and decides how to act on it. Because of this, you can control the narrative. Paint your target as a brutal criminal, or an innocent bystander. 

It's a bit of a short game, 3 or 4 hours max if you hit a few snags in your investigation, but its well worth the time and the money, even more so if you can catch it on sale. A solid 5/5

This game is quite a great surprise! Really simple, in terms of design -- it's really just a UI and a brief opening cinematic -- but brilliant in execution. 

I DESPERATELY wish that there was a way [i](perhaps after you've beaten it?)[/i] to rewind back a day. I played through it twice entirely, and the first few days several more times, to get achievements/outcomes which depend only on like 1 or 2 variables ... But that's only really a concern if you really want to get all the endings and achievements. [i](Or if you dislike playing through the "tutorial-esque" Day 1 over and over, like I do)[/i]. 

I highly recommend going into your playthroughs with a goal in mind -- whether you're going to be a government lackey or a rebel activist ... Doing a mixed approach nets less extremes and is a little less interesting, IMO. But it's neat that the snippets you discover have a rather noticeable impact on the game's events, characters, what info you're presented with, and the way everything shakes out. I love Telltale games but they could learn quite a bit from this indie studio. 

Anyway, if you enjoy solving mysteries and don't mind reading, this game is well worth your time!

This is it. This is the future of Games. A wonderful game that simulates a goverment investigator using a platform called Orwell to demistify the terror where your choices change every instance of the game. You will question yourself. Are you doing the right thing?

My though processes through playing this game:

"Alright, let's catch some terrorists"
"Oh shit I didn't mean to do that"
"No noonononoonono"
"I never meant for this to happen!"
"Fuck fuck fuck fuck"
"Oh shit."
After vaguely remembering this from a crowdfunding site whose name escapes me, I went into this game feeling like it would be a copy of the hacker simulators of the early 2000s, but I was pleasantly surprised.

I love this game. Not because of "social commentary" (Which is eerily close to what might be going on) Not because of the art style, or anything like that. But because that this is a game that, in a long while, made me feel like my choices really mattered. That a simple click and drag could mean either saving countless lives, or ending them. It made me feel like I was THAT guy behind that desk in a government building, torn between two choices, either ruining a life, or completely ignoring one. And when I realized that I had been chasing the wrong person the entire time, I felt like a failed detective, who chased that big case his entire life, only to be let down. 

No other game I have ever played, has made me feel like this. It really made me think about the choices I made, and also gave me 20/20 hindsight. And for $6, you can't go wrong with this captivating story. I never thought that I would be dragged into a game like this again after playing other mind-fuck games, but in all honesty, this game doesn't quite do that. It takes you to dinner first, then when you least expect it, you start to get drowsy, and you wake up in a daze at the end of this story, wondering what happened, and what went wrong. And oddly... you want to do it again.

I'm still in Episode 1. I'll get to the point immediately. So far I've found this game quite frustrating for two reasons:

1. Your "handler" does suspect interrogations.
He manages to make a complete ass of himself by pointlessly antagonising the suspects, and is saved only by the sheer volume of information you've painstakingly gathered. The in-universe explanation is that he has to act on pieces of information you have uploaded in Orwell, so while I'd like to see more dialog sophistication at such critical junctures (there's a method to do it, read it up online), I understand this would drive up design complexity, and therefore cost. Still that display of brute force was a bit annoying



2. Some things aren't as compartmentalised as you'd expect.
[spoiler]
You wouldn't expect an analyst to tell a strike team how to do their job, yet informing people on the ground of an impending danger might cause your handler to panic and instruct said strike team to go "all in", when in fact they should be the ones making the call. Where did they find this guy again? Anyway the resulting mess was his f-up, but of course you're the one who uploaded the intel, and you're the bloody player, so you're left feeling like it's your fault.


Also, when a suspect chooses to escape via the back window while the police are banging on the door, they shouldn't bee too surprised to find they're surrounded. Again, uploading that piece of intel felt like I was telling the strike team how to do their job... but frankly if they didn't know they're supposed to cover every exit, I might as well. They showed incompetence, and this frustrated me.

[/spoiler]


That said the game managed to get me emotionally invested (enough to write a review, yay!) so I'd definitely recommend it.

I'v just completed the first chapter and I'm not convinced the gameplay works for me.  It's a bit too linear.  I found pictures and details of suspects and contacts but couldn't upload them until the story unfolded enough for Orwell to recognise them as relevant data.  So for me it was a bit like when you get a game that says its 'open world' but then you find yourself prevented from exploring because of barriers a few inches high that for some reason you can't jump over.  In other words, frustrating!  Having said that, there were several very nice touches that made me smile and the game is definitely high quality.  If you are more patient than I am, you could easily enjoy this story with several endings.
To the developers, nice job but my suggestion for Orwell 2 is to allow the player to upload every sentence and picture (including irrelevant stuff) at any time to build a coherent case file and then submit it to Orwell for evaluation.

Incredibly well made game with a comfortable UI and naturally comfortable control of the UI, and a story that keeps me wanting to stay up to (in this case) "experience" the next chapter. I very much hope that a sequel will at least be considered.

I'll admit, I was skeptical, even with all the glowing reviews on Steam. However, bored with playing the same old games, I decided to give the game a try since it wasn't even 10$. As I started up the game, I asked myself - how this game could possibly keep me interested? It's a game where you're literally staring at a 'computer' screen in-game.. when you're already staring at a computer screen in real life. Not even 10 minutes in and I was hooked. I needed more information and I needed it NOW! I got really invested in the fictional characters stories, lives and background; why did she break up with him? How long were they dating? Why is 'X's relationship with her parents so strained? I looked through every single e-mail and chat message I could find. I listened to countless phone calls and actually cared what was said and listened intently. All the while snickering to myself because the fictional characters didn't know I was listening in on their conversations. 

This game proves that sometimes being innovative and creative pays off. The game was worth every last dollar. It's relatively short (6 hours) and  I played all the episodes straight through, but it still managed to keep me excited and interest throughout the whole game. I kept playing 'just 10 more minutes' to find new information. Although only 6 hours long, I felt like it's the perfect length. Any longer and I probably would have started getting annoyed (because I did want to find out the ending to the story). 

The only issues I had with the game was that it doesn't really explain how the 'upload information' works. It tells you very briefly what your job is - to upload information, but I didn't understand that I could literally choose what information to upload and what to withold. I thought I had to upload certain information to continue with the story - turns out that may not have necessarily been the case. I actually got an ending I didn't intend because even at the end of the game I wasn't really sure what I was supposed to be doing (how did I access information, not upload it but still continue with the story?). You would think 'upload information' would be an easy concept to understand and wouldn't really need a tutorial, but in my case I would have liked a proper 2-3 minute introduction to how Orwell 'works'. The fact that you can choose what you do and do not upload, and depending on that - there will be different concequences. 
The highlighting of relevant text kinda made the game too easy, but I do understand the necessity of the function. Any real-life program such as Orwell would probably have a similar feature that highlights relevant information. I felt like it made the game more realistic because occassionally while reading an on-going chat, I could quickly scan for relevant information that was highlighted - upload it - and then continue reading the conversation. 
I really idn't realize that my actions of uploading certain information would have concequences; I guess I thought the game was a lot more linear, not that I could actually influence what happened by what I did or did not upload. 

This was really unique, both in game-playstyle as well as story telling. I'll be playing it again, that's for sure.

[h1]Review:[/h1]
The most terrifying part of Orwell is just how easily its events could come to pass in our own world. George Orwell himself could not have predicted the level of surveillance we all voluntarily subject ourselves to by keeping always-listening, always-tracking smart devices on our persons, in our cars, and in our homes. It doesn’t take a lot of imagination to see a system such as the one portrayed in the game being used by a real nation, especially since we know the United States already conducts mass surveillance in a multitude of ways.


Orwell (the game) did an excellent job keeping me on the edge of my seat throughout its entire duration. Even though you only interact with them (or rather, their information) through a screen, it was hard not to feel connected to the characters. Whether that connection is based on sympathy or a desire to lock them up is up to you.


The game lends itself well to multiple playthroughs in order to achieve different endings, and there are tons of different ways to get to those endings. However, by the second or third time the first few chapters begin to feel very repetitive. I often found myself checking my phone while waiting for in-game conversations to finish so I could decide which chunks of data to grab. There is tons of interesting stuff to read in Orwell, but it would be nice to skip past some dialogue when I’ve already read it three times.


The length of the game really surprised me. For $11 I didn’t expect as much story and detail as I got. While it only took me about 6 hours my first time through, and I can definitely go through quicker now if I wanted, looking over all of the great little details that have been thrown in definitely takes time. That’s not a bad thing, as Orwell’s realism is only helped by how believable its characters (and their social media profiles, emails, and phone calls) are.


This is definitely a great game, and it was an awesome surprise when I discovered it while browsing the web one day. Be warned, though - after you play you’ll often find yourself thinking about your online conversations, and if something you said years ago (or even yesterday) could somehow be used to incriminate you.

Very engrossing game, I ended up playing it for 4 hours straight just to see the ending. I'll likely return to it for a second playthrough too, as the decisions you make have both immediate and long-term impacts on what happens in the game.
